structure.title: Sections 1–3 · The opening distinction
structure.text: Epictetus separates what depends on us from what can be taken away despite our best efforts. He immediately gives the distinction a cost. It includes the body, possessions and the opinions of people whose approval matters to us.

structure.title: Sections 4–32 · A series of rehearsals
structure.text: A bathhouse, a dinner invitation and a broken cup give the student occasions to practise before the stakes rise. Epictetus repeatedly changes the example until the reader meets the same principle where assent comes less easily.

structure.title: Sections 33–52 · The difficulty of becoming a student
structure.text: Rules about talk, meals, company and teaching turn the scrutiny back on the person learning philosophy. Knowing how to explain an author can itself become a prize that distracts a student from doing what the explanation requires.

people.name: Judgment
people.role: What happens after the first appearance
people.text: Someone insults you. Epictetus is interested in the moment you agree that what happened has damaged the part of your life that matters most. Exercises throughout the manual try to make that moment available for inspection.

people.name: A role
people.text: Being a child, sibling or neighbour places claims on a person's conduct. Those claims can survive another person's failure to play their part well, which makes these instructions much harder than advice to seek agreeable company.

context.title: A handbook for practice
context.text: Arrian collected Epictetus's teaching into a short manual. Abrupt instructions often condense arguments a pupil might have heard elsewhere. Their wording makes them portable enough to recall in the middle of a disappointment.

context.title: What lies within a choice
context.text: Epictetus opens with a distinction he will need even for a dinner invitation. You can choose what to offer a host in return for his favour. The invitation itself belongs to the host to give. Trouble begins when something in the second category feels so important that you treat it as a possession somebody has taken from you.

passages.quote: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.

notice.text: Compare a stranger's loss with your own.
notice.why: Advice that sounds reasonable when the neighbour breaks a cup takes on a different weight in your own house. Epictetus uses that asymmetry to expose which judgments change when ownership enters the picture.

notice.text: Notice what the dinner invitation costs.
notice.why: Getting invited might require flattering the host. Epictetus asks the disappointed guest to count the price they declined to pay as carefully as the meal they missed.

opening: Someone insults you, a plan falls apart, a person whose approval you wanted looks elsewhere. Epictetus treats these ordinary injuries as evidence of a dangerous arrangement: your peace depends on things other people can withhold. A former slave, he proposes a discipline severe enough to survive that discovery. His instructions keep returning responsibility to judgments and choices, even when circumstances are brutal. The difficulty begins where the advice gets specific, asking what you are prepared to stop demanding from the world.
